domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What hemodynamic definition characterizes cardiac tamponade, and what physical examination finding reflects equalization of diastolic pressures?
answer: Tamponade is hemodynamic insufficiency from impaired cardiac filling due to pericardial pressure; equalization of diastolic pressures produces elevated JVP with prominent x descent and absent y descent, plus pulsus paradoxus.
rationale: Pericardial fluid increases intrapericardial pressure, compressing all chambers; during inspiration venous return to the right heart increases but leftward septal shift limits LV filling, causing the characteristic paradoxical pulse.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Cardiac tamponade should be suspected in any patient with cardiac arrest after what clinical context, and what emergency intervention confirms and treats it simultaneously?
answer: Tamponade should be suspected in cardiac arrest of unclear cause; pericardiocentesis—ideally guided by POCUS—both confirms tamponade (fluid withdrawal) and relieves it.
rationale: In traumatic or malignant tamponade, pericardiocentesis can restore cardiac output immediately; POCUS guidance increases procedural safety and diagnostic accuracy.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Hyperviscosity syndrome from plasma cell dyscrasias can cause which cardiopulmonary complications that may mimic cardiac tamponade?
answer: High-output cardiac failure, shortness of breath, and valvular dysfunction; these occur less commonly than neurologic symptoms in hyperviscosity.
rationale: Increased blood viscosity raises cardiac afterload and reduces microvascular flow; in severe cases myocardial oxygen delivery falls, causing high-output failure or ischemia.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  hyperviscosity syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: On point-of-care ultrasound, what probe and position are used to identify pericardial effusion in a supine ICU patient?
answer: The phased array (cardiac) probe at the subxiphoid or parasternal long-axis view identifies pericardial effusion as an echo-free space surrounding the heart; the subxiphoid view is most accessible in supine critically ill patients.
rationale: POCUS for tamponade assessment shows right ventricular diastolic collapse (earliest sign) and IVC plethora as hemodynamically significant findings.
confusable_with: Pleural effusion (posterior to heart on parasternal view)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What cancers most commonly produce pericardial metastases leading to tamponade?
answer: Cancers of the kidney, breast, ovary, testis, colon, rectum, head and neck, and uterus; metastases may be present in pericardial tissue or lymph nodes.
rationale: Hematogenous or lymphatic spread to the pericardium causes malignant effusion; highly vascular or lymphophilic tumors have the highest rates of pericardial involvement.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: In venoarterial ECMO used for cardiogenic shock, how is venous blood handled?
answer: Venous blood is removed from the patient, oxygenated and CO2-extracted extracorporeally, then reinfused into the arterial system, effectively replacing both heart and lung function.
rationale: VA-ECMO provides full cardiopulmonary bypass outside the operating room; it is used for refractory cardiogenic shock including tamponade while awaiting definitive drainage or surgical repair.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Pericardial disease affects ventricular preload through what mechanism?
answer: Increased pericardial pressure is a factor affecting ventricular preload (along with blood volume, intrathoracic pressure, venous tone, and heart rate); tamponade raises pericardial pressure and directly limits cardiac filling.
rationale: Ventricular preload depends on transmural filling pressure; pericardial pressure adds to intracardiac pressure, reducing the transmural gradient and chamber filling.

enabling_conditions: Known malignancy (especially lung, breast, lymphoma, leukemia), pericarditis, recent cardiac surgery, uremia, trauma
pathophysiology: Pericardial fluid accumulation raises intrapericardial pressure; when pericardial pressure equals ventricular filling pressure, diastolic collapse occurs, cardiac output falls, and obstructive shock ensues
time_course: Can develop acutely (hemopericardium) or subacutely (malignant effusion); cardiac output falls when ~250 mL accumulates rapidly or >1000 mL accumulates slowly
key_features: Beck's triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds); pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; POCUS: effusion + RV diastolic collapse + IVC plethora
consequence_if_missed: Pulseless electrical activity cardiac arrest; death within minutes of complete cardiac compression without pericardiocentesis

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Approximately 90% of all hypercalcemia cases are due to which two etiologies?
answer: Malignancy and hyperparathyroidism account for approximately 90% of all hypercalcemia; malignancy is the most common cause in hospitalized patients.
rationale: Hyperparathyroidism predominates in outpatient/ambulatory settings; malignancy-associated hypercalcemia, though less common overall, is the leading cause among hospitalized patients due to their sicker population.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What distinguishes the PTH level in malignancy-associated hypercalcemia from hyperparathyroidism?
answer: In malignancy, serum PTH is suppressed (due to negative feedback from elevated calcium); in hyperparathyroidism, PTH is elevated (autonomous secretion despite high calcium).
rationale: Measuring PTH first differentiates the two most common causes; suppressed PTH with high calcium points to PTHrP-mediated or other malignancy mechanisms, directing workup toward PTHrP and 1,25-OH vitamin D levels.
confusable_with: PTHrP (not measured by standard PTH assay)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What is the first-line treatment for symptomatic hypercalcemia, and what second-line agents are used for hypercalcemia of malignancy specifically?
answer: First-line: rehydration with IV normal saline followed by brisk diuresis. Second-line for malignancy: IV bisphosphonates (pamidronate or etidronate) to inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
rationale: Volume expansion dilutes calcium and enhances renal excretion; bisphosphonates address the underlying mechanism of osteoclast activation by myeloma or osteolytic metastases.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: In hypercalcemia of hyperparathyroidism, what calcium target should be achieved with hydration and diuresis before proceeding with parathyroidectomy?
answer: Serum calcium should be decreased to below 14 mg/dL (7 mEq/L or 3.5 mmol/L) with IV normal saline and furosemide-facilitated diuresis before surgery.
rationale: Severe hypercalcemia impairs cardiac conduction, neuromuscular function, and renal concentrating ability; reducing calcium before anesthesia decreases arrhythmia risk and improves organ function.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy is mediated by which peptide, and when should 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D be measured?
answer: PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related peptide) mediates humoral hypercalcemia; if PTHrP is low, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D should be measured to screen for vitamin D-mediated hypercalcemia (e.g., granulomatous disease, lymphoma).
rationale: PTHrP mimics PTH at its receptor, causing bone resorption and renal calcium retention; when absent, alternative mechanisms (1,25-OH-D from granulomas or lymphoma) must be sought.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Hypercalcemia  Causes and Management

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Hypercalcemia may promote which systemic complications beyond neurological and renal effects?
answer: Pancreatitis, peptic ulcer disease (calcium stimulates gastrin secretion), kidney failure, and sensitization to digoxin toxicity.
rationale: Hypercalcemia activates multiple end-organ effects: pancreatic ductal obstruction and enzyme activation, gastric acid secretion, nephrocalcinosis/nephrogenic DI, and enhanced cardiac Na/K-ATPase inhibition by digitalis.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Vitamin D metabolism involves conversion through which two sequential hydroxylation steps, and which enzyme in the second step is ectopically active in granulomatous disease?
answer: First: 7-dehydrocalciferol to vitamin D3 via UV light; then 25-hydroxylation in liver; then 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts 25-OH-D to active 1,25-OH-D. In granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, lymphoma), macrophages express ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase, overproducing active vitamin D.
rationale: Ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase in activated macrophages escapes normal feedback regulation, continuously producing 1,25-OH-D which drives intestinal calcium absorption and hypercalcemia.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What four metabolic disturbances define tumor lysis syndrome, and which end-organ complications result?
answer: Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and hyperuricemia; end-organ complications include acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmias, and death.
rationale: Massive tumor cell lysis releases intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids (metabolized to uric acid); phosphate binds calcium causing hypocalcemia; uric acid and calcium-phosphate crystals obstruct renal tubules.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

confusable_with: Spontaneous tumor lysis (can occur without chemotherapy)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: In laboratory TLS, what was the most common electrolyte finding, and in clinical TLS, which complication predominated?
answer: Laboratory TLS most commonly showed hyperuricemia (52%); clinical TLS most commonly involved renal insufficiency (62.5%) and cardiac arrhythmias (35.9%).
rationale: Uric acid elevation is the most sensitive early marker; renal failure and arrhythmias represent end-organ consequences that define clinical severity.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Rasburicase works by what mechanism, and how does this differ from allopurinol in treating hyperuricemia in TLS?
answer: Rasburicase converts existing uric acid to allantoin, rapidly reducing uric acid levels; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase to prevent new uric acid formation but does not lower existing levels.
rationale: In acute TLS, pre-formed uric acid must be rapidly eliminated to prevent renal tubular obstruction; only rasburicase can reduce existing uric acid, while allopurinol is useful for prevention.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Why is urine alkalinization controversial despite increasing uric acid solubility 10-fold in TLS management?
answer: Urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate increases uric acid solubility but reduces ionized calcium levels, risking symptomatic hypocalcemia and xanthine crystallization; it is no longer routinely recommended.
rationale: Alkalinization shifts calcium equilibrium toward non-ionized forms, worsening the hypocalcemia already present from hyperphosphatemia; the risk-benefit ratio is unfavorable when rasburicase is available.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Uric acid obstructive uropathy in TLS can impede potassium excretion by what mechanism, and what is the life-threatening consequence?
answer: Uric acid crystals obstruct renal tubules, reducing GFR and potassium excretion, leading to life-threatening hyperkalemia with risk of cardiac arrest from arrhythmias.
rationale: The kidney is the primary route for potassium excretion; when uric acid nephropathy reduces GFR, the massive potassium released from lysed tumor cells accumulates, causing potentially fatal ventricular arrhythmias.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: A key limitation of the Cairo-Bishop TLS definition is what clinical reality?
answer: The definition requires chemotherapy initiation, but TLS can develop spontaneously before any treatment is given; this excludes spontaneous TLS from the formal diagnostic criteria.
rationale: Spontaneous TLS occurs in highly proliferative tumors (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL); recognition requires clinical vigilance in high-risk patients even before therapy, not just post-chemotherapy monitoring.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: In patients with preexisting kidney or cardiac conditions who develop TLS, what modification to standard aggressive hydration is required?
answer: Careful fluid management with monitoring for fluid overload; diuretics may be used to support urine output; in severe cases renal replacement therapy may be needed.
rationale: Aggressive hydration is the cornerstone of TLS prevention/treatment, but patients with reduced cardiac or renal reserve cannot handle high fluid volumes; individualized fluid management prevents pulmonary edema.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Oncologic emergencies  tumor lysis syndrome

enabling_conditions: High tumor burden (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, large DLBCL), rapid proliferation rate, high LDH, renal insufficiency at baseline, after initiation of cytotoxic therapy
pathophysiology: Massive tumor cell lysis releases K+, phosphate, nucleic acids (uric acid precursors) into circulation; hyperphosphatemia chelates calcium (hypocalcemia); uric acid and calcium-phosphate crystals obstruct renal tubules causing AKI
time_course: Develops 12-72 hours after chemotherapy initiation; spontaneous TLS in highly proliferative tumors; peaks 24-48h post-treatment
key_features: Cairo-Bishop criteria: hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia; clinical TLS adds AKI, cardiac arrhythmia, seizure, or death
consequence_if_missed: Fatal ventricular arrhythmia from hyperkalemia; acute renal failure requiring dialysis; tetanic seizures from hypocalcemia

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: What are the four major local complications of acute pancreatitis, and which requires drainage if symptomatic or infected?
answer: Pancreatic edema (resolves), necrosis (high infection risk), pseudocyst (encapsulated fluid—requires drainage if symptomatic/infected/compressing), and abscess (requires drainage plus antibiotics).
rationale: Local complications span a severity spectrum; necrosis is the most serious, with infected necrosis carrying 30-40% mortality; pseudocysts and abscesses require interventional drainage to prevent septic complications.
confusable_with: Walled-off necrosis (mature necrosis, distinct from pseudocyst)

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: What are the three most common causes of acute pancreatitis listed by frequency in male vs. female sex?
answer: Overall: gallstones/sludge 40-75% (#1 in female sex), alcohol 30% (#1 in male sex), hypertriglyceridemia (TG>1000) 10% (#3); anatomic and drug-induced causes less common.
rationale: Sex-specific etiology differences reflect behavioral (alcohol) and metabolic (gallstone risk with female hormones) patterns; hypertriglyceridemia is an important and often missed cause when TG exceeds 1000 mg/dL.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: When is urgent ERCP indicated in acute pancreatitis?
answer: When clinical or diagnostic findings indicate biliary obstruction or cholangitis (e.g., rising bilirubin, biliary dilation, fever); not routinely for all gallstone pancreatitis.
rationale: ERCP removes obstructing common bile duct stones and relieves biliary pressure; in uncomplicated gallstone pancreatitis without ongoing obstruction or cholangitis, ERCP adds risk without benefit.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Overall mortality of acute pancreatitis is approximately 1-2%, but rises substantially in which specific subgroup?
answer: Mortality rises substantially in severe acute pancreatitis (organ failure, infected necrosis); the overall figure obscures the high mortality in severe cases.
rationale: Mild interstitial pancreatitis has near-zero mortality; necrotizing pancreatitis with persistent organ failure or infected necrosis carries 15-40% mortality despite modern ICU care.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: In post-operative hepatic dysfunction, what are the major causes to consider?
answer: Viral hepatitis, impaired hepatic perfusion, preexisting liver disease, hepatocyte hypoxia, sepsis, hemolysis, benign postoperative cholestasis, and drug-induced hepatotoxicity (including halothane hepatitis with repeated exposure).
rationale: Multiple insults may coexist perioperatively; distinguishing ischemic hepatitis (rising transaminases, low output state) from drug-induced or viral hepatitis requires correlation with clinical context and timing.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Alcohol-related pancreatitis is more common in which socioeconomic group, and what is the recurrence rate if the underlying cause is not addressed?
answer: Alcohol-related pancreatitis is more common in lower-income populations; the recurrence rate is high if alcohol use continues; gallstone-related cases are more frequent in older adults and those with obesity/metabolic syndrome.
rationale: Recurrence drives progression to chronic pancreatitis and its complications (exocrine/endocrine insufficiency, pain, malignancy risk); etiology-specific management (cessation, cholecystectomy) is essential to prevent recurrence.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: In chronic pancreatitis, obstructing pancreatic stones may be extracted by what interventional approaches when traditional basket extraction fails?
answer: ESWL (extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy), pancreatoscopy-assisted laser lithotripsy, or electrohydraulic lithotripsy may be used when traditional extraction fails; children may have softer stones extractable by basket.
rationale: Pancreatic duct stones obstruct flow, causing upstream hypertension and pain; fragmentation by ESWL makes stones small enough for endoscopic extraction, relieving obstruction and reducing pain.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What is the normal pericardial fluid volume, and what is the basic physiologic function of the pericardium?
answer: 20-50 mL of pericardial fluid in adults; the pericardium surrounds the heart but is not normally adherent, limiting intrapericardiac volume and preventing excessive cardiac dilatation.
rationale: The inextensible fibrous pericardium constrains acute cardiac enlargement (preventing overdistension) and couples ventricular filling, so disease affecting it has major hemodynamic consequences.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: Constrictive pericarditis presents with what classic physical examination triad, and how is the venous waveform pattern different from tamponade?
answer: JVD, hepatomegaly, and often ascites; constrictive pericarditis shows a prominent y descent on the CVP waveform (rapid early diastolic filling), whereas tamponade shows an absent y descent.
rationale: In constriction, the rigid pericardium limits late diastolic filling but allows early rapid filling (prominent y descent); in tamponade, fluid prevents filling throughout diastole, abolishing the y descent.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: Volatile anesthetics provide myocardial protection via what molecular mechanism that is relevant to ischemic pericarditis patients?
answer: Volatile anesthetics activate ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels, providing ischemic preconditioning; they may also enhance recovery of stunned myocardium after ischemia.
rationale: KATP channel activation mimics ischemic preconditioning by inducing a protected state that reduces calcium overload and mitochondrial injury during ischemia-reperfusion.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What factors affecting ventricular preload are categorized together in the context of cardiac physiology?
answer: Blood volume, distribution of blood volume, intrathoracic pressure, pericardial pressure, venous tone, heart rhythm (atrial contraction), and heart rate all determine ventricular preload.
rationale: Preload is the ventricular end-diastolic filling pressure; any factor that alters venous return or cardiac filling contributes, so pericardial disease is one of several preload determinants.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: In constrictive pericarditis, what abnormalities of liver function and abdominal examination are commonly found?
answer: Liver function may be abnormal (congestive hepatopathy from chronic venous congestion); hepatomegaly and ascites are present due to elevated right-sided filling pressures.
rationale: Chronically elevated right atrial pressure from constrictive pericarditis causes venous hypertension in the hepatic sinusoids, resulting in hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, and transudative ascites.
confusable_with: Right heart failure from other causes

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: Point-of-care ultrasound can diagnose what three emergency conditions simultaneously in an undifferentiated dyspneic patient?
answer: Pericardial effusion/tamponade, pleural effusion, and pneumothorax can all be identified by POCUS in an undifferentiated dyspneic or shocked patient.
rationale: POCUS integrates cardiac, lung, and pleural assessment into a rapid bedside protocol, allowing simultaneous identification of treatable emergency diagnoses that would require multiple separate imaging studies otherwise.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: After cardiac surgery, what pericardial complication can onset 6-24 hours postoperatively and mimic malignant hyperthermia initially?
answer: Thyroid storm can onset 6-24 hours after surgery (from stress-induced thyroid hormone release), but unlike MH it responds to antithyroid agents and does not cause muscular rigidity.
rationale: Surgical stress precipitates thyroid storm in unrecognized hyperthyroidism; the timing post-surgery, fever, and tachycardia overlap with MH, but the absence of rigidity and response to beta-blockade/antithyroid drugs distinguishes them.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What is the standard prophylactic dose of unfractionated heparin (UFH) for non-orthopedic surgical patients, and in what renal situation is UFH preferred over LMWH?
answer: UFH 5000 units subcutaneously 2-3 times daily; UFH is preferred in patients with low GFR (renal insufficiency) because it does not accumulate with renal failure unlike LMWH.
rationale: LMWH is renally cleared and accumulates in CKD, increasing bleeding risk; UFH is metabolized independent of renal function and is safer in severe renal impairment.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Antithrombotic prophylaxis reduces perioperative VTE risk, and what dual monitoring concern exists specifically with UFH prophylaxis?
answer: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) should be monitored by platelet count checks; HIT can paradoxically cause thrombosis despite anticoagulation.
rationale: UFH binds platelet factor 4, occasionally triggering an IgG antibody that activates platelets and causes paradoxical thrombosis (HIT type 2); platelet monitoring every 2-3 days detects the characteristic platelet fall.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: In cancer patients hospitalized for acute illness, what special consideration applies to VTE prophylaxis compared to general medical patients?
answer: DVT prophylaxis is indicated in hospitalized cancer patients; UFH or LMWH is used, with the dose potentially increased (UFH 5000-7500 units 3 times daily in high-risk patients) due to the hypercoagulable state of malignancy.
rationale: Cancer-associated hypercoagulability (Trousseau syndrome) arises from tumor-derived procoagulants, tissue factor expression, and treatment-related factors; standard prophylactic doses may be insufficient.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Aspirin may be used as a hybrid VTE prophylaxis strategy in what surgical context?
answer: In non-orthopedic surgeries, aspirin can be used in hybrid regimens where parenteral agents are used in-hospital and aspirin substituted at discharge for extended outpatient prophylaxis.
rationale: Aspirin's antiplatelet mechanism provides partial VTE risk reduction with lower bleeding risk and simpler oral dosing than LMWH or DOAC for outpatient extended prophylaxis in selected patients.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: In a patient with liver cirrhosis being evaluated for VTE prophylaxis, why is a standard INR-based assessment insufficient?
answer: In cirrhosis, procoagulation factors may not be impaired as much as anticoagulation factors; additional assessment is needed before withholding VTE prophylaxis based on an elevated INR alone.
rationale: The cirrhotic liver reduces both pro- and anticoagulant factor synthesis; the net coagulation balance may not be predicted by the INR, which primarily reflects procoagulant factors, leading to under-appreciation of thrombotic risk.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Preoperative fasting combined with surgical stress induces what metabolic change that is directly relevant to VTE and glucose management?
answer: Preoperative fasting and surgical stress induce insulin resistance; patients who are not allowed clear fluids after overnight fast are more insulin resistant than those given a carbohydrate load.
rationale: Insulin resistance impairs glucose disposal and promotes hyperglycemia; hyperglycemia increases platelet activation and inflammatory markers, compounding VTE risk in surgical patients.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Perioperative management of patients on chronic anticoagulation requires a multidisciplinary team approach. Who are the key stakeholders?
answer: The patient, primary care physician, hematologist, surgeon, and anesthesia provider; careful preoperative assessment of antithrombotic therapy with bridging decisions made collaboratively.
rationale: Individual specialists have conflicting priorities (bleeding vs. thrombosis); the anesthesiologist must understand all anticoagulants to plan safe neuraxial anesthesia timing and reversal options.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: In the ACC/AHA perioperative algorithm, what is done after determining a patient has LOW estimated perioperative risk of MACE (<1%)?
answer: Proceed to surgery without further cardiac testing; additional workup is reserved for elevated-risk patients where testing may change management.
rationale: Low-risk patients have a favorable risk-benefit ratio for proceeding; additional testing creates delays, costs, and potential complications without improving outcomes when baseline risk is already low.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Intraoperative ST-segment elevation or depression increases perioperative cardiac event risk by how much, and tachycardia over 120 bpm for 5 minutes postoperatively increases death risk by how much?
answer: ST changes increase cardiac event risk 10-fold and death risk 2-fold; tachycardia above 120 bpm for 5 minutes postoperatively increases death risk 10-fold.
rationale: These data emphasize that intraoperative monitoring and postoperative tachycardia control are not merely technical goals but have profound survival implications.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Increasing frailty in geriatric patients is associated with what perioperative outcomes?
answer: Increasing frailty is associated with higher morbidity and mortality; frailty is best viewed as an overall risk assessment integrating age and disease-related factors across multiple organ systems.
rationale: Frailty represents physiologic reserve depletion; reduced reserve amplifies the stress of surgery, impairs recovery, and predicts complications beyond what chronological age or single-organ assessment captures.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Hypertension is a major global cause of death and a perioperative risk factor. What is the primary cardiovascular concern with undertreated perioperative hypertension?
answer: Hypertension is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and end-stage renal disease; perioperatively, labile or undertreated hypertension increases myocardial ischemia, stroke, and aortic complications.
rationale: Hypertension increases left ventricular wall stress and oxygen demand; intraoperative swings in blood pressure in hypertensive patients exceed those in normotensive patients, increasing ischemic risk.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What is the most common cause of end-stage renal disease, and how does this affect perioperative cardiovascular risk assessment?
answer: Diabetes is the most common cause of ESRD, followed by hypertension and glomerulonephritis; CKD/ESRD patients have markedly elevated cardiovascular event risk that must be factored into pre-surgical risk stratification.
rationale: Uremia causes accelerated atherosclerosis, impaired platelet function, anemia, and volume dysregulation; patients with CKD undergoing surgery have substantially higher MACE rates than the general population.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: In the PACU, what renal complications warrant diagnostic attention with focus on readily reversible causes?
answer: Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h) in the PACU requires evaluation for prerenal (hypovolemia), intrinsic renal (intraoperative insult exacerbating CKD), and postrenal (catheter obstruction) causes.
rationale: Prompt identification and correction of prerenal oliguria (IV fluids, optimize cardiac output) prevents progression to ischemic ATN; unrecognized obstruction similarly causes preventable acute kidney injury.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: No specific preoperative laboratory studies are recommended solely on the basis of age in geriatric patients. What minimum evaluation is recommended?
answer: Careful assessment of cardiac, pulmonary, and renal systems should be performed at minimum before any procedure in geriatric patients; no age-based blanket ordering is supported.
rationale: Evidence does not support routine comprehensive testing in all elderly patients; targeted testing based on identified comorbidities avoids unnecessary delays, costs, and cascade effects of false-positive results.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Diabetes mellitus increases perioperative complication risk through what specific mechanisms?
answer: Hyperglycemia is associated with cardiovascular events and infectious complications including wound infection, pneumonia, and sepsis; DM also causes autonomic neuropathy affecting hemodynamic stability.
rationale: Hyperglycemia impairs leukocyte function (phagocytosis and chemotaxis), promotes bacterial growth, delays wound healing, and causes endothelial dysfunction that worsens ischemic injury.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What HbA1c threshold is relevant to preventing surgical site infections, and what skin preparation is recommended?
answer: Specific HbA1c targets for SSI prevention are cited in CDC guidelines; patients should shower with soap or an antiseptic agent at least the night before surgery regardless of diabetic status.
rationale: Perioperative hyperglycemia is a modifiable SSI risk factor; preoperative HbA1c reflects glycemic control and predicts wound complication rates; skin decolonization reduces bacterial burden at the incision site.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Patients on maintenance buprenorphine undergoing surgery present a specific opioid management challenge. What perioperative approach is now recommended?
answer: Maintain the patient on a stable buprenorphine dose perioperatively; additional full agonist opioids may be titrated on top of buprenorphine for acute pain management rather than stopping buprenorphine preoperatively.
rationale: Stopping buprenorphine risks opioid use disorder relapse and poorly managed acute pain; buprenorphine's partial agonism and ceiling effect do not fully block acute opioid analgesia when full agonists are titrated appropriately.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Multimodal perioperative analgesia is a broad strategy. What modalities are included?
answer: Combination of interventional techniques (epidural, peripheral nerve blocks/catheters), IV infusions (ketamine, lidocaine), patient-controlled analgesia (oral, IV, SC), and non-opioid adjuncts (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, gabapentinoids).
rationale: Multimodal analgesia exploits different analgesic mechanisms to achieve adequate pain control with lower doses of each agent, reducing opioid-related side effects (respiratory depression, ileus, nausea).

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: There are no antidotes for which class of anticoagulants, making bridging decisions and procedural timing especially critical?
answer: Direct thrombin inhibitors (DTIs, e.g., argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran) have no specific antidotes; reversal depends on drug clearance. Note: idarucizumab reverses dabigatran specifically.
rationale: The absence of a universal antidote for DTIs means bleeding complications require supportive care and time-dependent drug clearance; procedural timing must account for each agent's half-life and renal function.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Antiparkinsonian drugs and tricyclic antidepressants both have what side effect that is pharmacologically important when combined with anesthetic medications?
answer: Anticholinergic side effects; they augment the sedation produced by scopolamine and other anticholinergics, and tricyclics also inhibit neuronal catecholamine reuptake.
rationale: The combined anticholinergic burden from multiple drugs causes additive cognitive impairment, tachycardia, urinary retention, and ileus; recognizing this interaction prevents perioperative delirium and autonomic instability.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Remifentanil and alfentanil are preferred when what clinical goal is needed for opioid dosing?
answer: When a brief duration of opioid effect followed by rapid dissipation is required; remifentanil's context-sensitive half-time remains very short regardless of infusion duration due to ester hydrolysis.
rationale: Remifentanil is metabolized by non-specific plasma and tissue esterases, independent of hepatic/renal function; this allows rapid offset even after prolonged infusion, ideal for procedures requiring intraoperative analgesia with fast awakening.
confusable_with: Fentanyl (longer context-sensitive half-time with prolonged infusion)

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What preoperative interventions in COPD patients have been shown to decrease postoperative pulmonary complications?
answer: Correcting hypoxemia, relieving bronchospasm, mobilizing and reducing secretions, and treating active infections preoperatively decrease the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications.
rationale: COPD patients have baseline airflow obstruction and mucus hypersecretion; optimization before surgery reduces the incremental impairment caused by anesthesia, pain-related splinting, and postoperative immobility.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Preventing postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) is a key goal in the perioperative period. What patient and procedure factors most increase PPC risk?
answer: OSA, COPD, obesity, prolonged thoracic or upper abdominal surgery, general anesthesia, prolonged procedure duration, and emergency surgery are major PPC risk factors.
rationale: Thoracic and upper abdominal surgery directly impairs diaphragm function and FRC; added to baseline respiratory compromise (OSA, COPD, obesity), these create high risk for atelectasis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: OSA patients who are noncompliant with PAP therapy have elevated serum bicarbonate preoperatively. What does this indicate and how should surgery be managed?
answer: Elevated serum bicarbonate indicates chronic hypoventilation with renal bicarbonate compensation (OHS or severe OSA); these patients need especially careful preoperative pulmonary evaluation and should resume PAP therapy.
rationale: Metabolic alkalosis from chronic CO2 retention signals severely impaired baseline respiratory function; these patients are at extreme risk for postoperative respiratory failure and may require prolonged PACU/HDU monitoring.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What is the appropriate perioperative pain management strategy that also reduces postoperative pulmonary complications?
answer: Epidural analgesia or regional nerve blocks combined with systemic multimodal analgesia reduce opioid use, minimize respiratory depression, and improve pain-related splinting—collectively reducing PPCs.
rationale: Neuraxial and regional techniques provide excellent analgesia without systemic opioid depression of respiratory drive; adequate analgesia also enables deep breathing and effective coughing, preventing atelectasis.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: HFNC compared to standard oxygen therapy or NIV in patients with hypoxemic respiratory failure was associated with what outcome in one major trial?
answer: HFNC reduced mortality compared to standard oxygen therapy or NIV in patients with hypoxemic respiratory failure, though it did not reduce the rate of tracheal intubation.
rationale: HFNC delivers high-flow humidified oxygen with a low level of CPAP effect, improving oxygenation and reducing respiratory work; the survival benefit without intubation reduction suggests benefit through mechanisms beyond preventing intubation.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: What specific preoperative imaging consideration applies to patients with cardiac devices (pacemakers, ICDs) scheduled for extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL)?
answer: Patients with cardiac arrhythmias, pacemakers, or ICDs may be at risk for device-triggered arrhythmias from shock wave energy during ESWL; device interrogation and programming adjustment may be required.
rationale: ESWL shock waves can trigger electrical artifacts sensed by pacemakers/ICDs as shockable rhythms; inappropriate ICD shocks or pacemaker inhibition can occur, requiring device management before the procedure.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: When is medical management prior to surgery considered sufficient for patients with concurrent cardiopulmonary disease undergoing non-cardiac surgery?
answer: A thorough, focused history and physical examination through the lens of the perioperative specialist serves as the basis for evaluation; advanced testing is ordered only when it will change management.
rationale: Routine preoperative testing has not been shown to improve outcomes; targeted assessment of functional capacity and disease-specific risk guides selective testing and is more cost-effective.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What coagulation factor deficiencies are most commonly seen after cardiopulmonary bypass, and how are they corrected?
answer: Factors V and VIII are most commonly depleted during CPB; if clinically significant bleeding occurs, fresh frozen plasma is the treatment of choice.
rationale: CPB dilutes and consumes coagulation factors through hemodilution and platelet-surface activation; the labile Factors V and VIII are disproportionately depleted and must be replaced with FFP.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: In damage control resuscitation for massive trauma, what ratio of blood products has been shown to improve survival?
answer: Balanced administration of red blood cells, FFP, and platelets (1:1:1 ratio) to recreate whole blood has been associated with improved survival in trauma resuscitation.
rationale: Early coagulopathy of trauma depletes all coagulation factors simultaneously; balanced resuscitation prevents the dilutional coagulopathy that occurs when only pRBCs and crystalloids are given.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Prolonged PT in a preoperative patient should be evaluated with mixing studies. What does a corrected PT in mixing studies indicate vs. a non-corrected PT?
answer: Correction of PT after mixing with normal plasma indicates a factor deficiency; failure to correct indicates an inhibitor (e.g., lupus anticoagulant, factor-specific inhibitor, fibrin degradation products) is present.
rationale: Factor deficiencies are diluted by normal plasma and the PT corrects; inhibitors bind/neutralize the added factors and prevent correction, directing workup toward immunologic vs. replacement treatment.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Patients with obstructive jaundice, intestinal obstruction, or bowel resection are at risk for deficiency of which vitamin, and what coagulation consequence follows?
answer: Vitamin K deficiency; gut microbiota are a source of vitamin K synthesis, and fat malabsorption or bowel dysfunction reduces vitamin K absorption, causing factors II, VII, IX, X deficiency and prolonged PT.
rationale: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and requires bile salts for absorption; the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors (II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S) require it for carboxylation and activation.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: When a percutaneous transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is placed, what coagulation-related risk may the concomitant nitroglycerin infusion mitigate?
answer: Concomitant IV nitroglycerin may reduce the likelihood of right heart complications and bleeding associated with TIPS; the procedure's venous access and shunting can cause right heart pressure changes.
rationale: TIPS creation rapidly increases right heart preload by redirecting portal blood into systemic circulation; nitroglycerin reduces venous return and right heart strain while also reducing TIPS-associated bleeding complications.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Leukoreduction of blood products is performed to prevent what specific complications in chronically transfused patients?
answer: Leukoreduction prevents HLA alloimmunization in chronically transfused patients, bone marrow or kidney/heart/lung transplant candidates, reducing febrile non-hemolytic reactions and platelet refractoriness.
rationale: Donor leukocytes express HLA antigens; repeated exposure generates HLA antibodies that destroy subsequent transfused platelets (platelet refractoriness) and can cause febrile reactions and CMV transmission.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Sodium solutions used for diluting pRBCs during transfusion should be what type, and what is the risk with large-volume normal saline?
answer: Normal saline (NS) is preferred for diluting pRBCs (LR contains calcium which can cause clotting); large volumes of NS produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis and risk of AKI.
rationale: Chloride loading from NS inhibits renal vasodilatation (afferent arteriole constriction via tubuloglomerular feedback), reduces GFR, and produces a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
confusable_with: Lactated Ringer's (cannot be used with blood products)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: A single unit of platelets is expected to increase the platelet count by how much, and an apheresis unit by how much?
answer: A single unit raises platelet count by 5,000-10,000 x10^9/L; a platelet apheresis unit raises it by 30,000-60,000 x10^9/L.
rationale: Apheresis platelets contain the equivalent of 6-8 random donor units from a single donor, reducing alloimmunization risk while providing a larger incremental count increase.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: What is the Stanford massive transfusion guideline composition, and why is the platelet ratio lower than the 1:1:1 damage control ratio?
answer: Stanford MTG provides 6 pRBCs, 4 FFP, and 1 unit of platelets; the ratio reflects practical product availability and takes 30 minutes to prepare, approximating balanced resuscitation.
rationale: Perfect 1:1:1 ratio is the ideal; institutional protocols balance this against product availability, preparation time, and blood bank logistics while maintaining the essential principle of early plasma and platelet co-administration.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: The bleeding time as a preoperative test has what limitations with respect to predicting surgical bleeding?
answer: A normal bleeding time does NOT predict adequate hemostasis during surgery, and an abnormal bleeding time does NOT reliably predict excessive surgical bleeding; the test is poorly reproducible and should not guide transfusion decisions.
rationale: Bleeding time measures skin capillary plug formation under standardized conditions that poorly replicate surgical hemostasis; platelet function assays or viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) are more clinically relevant.
confusable_with: TEG platelet mapping (better predictor of platelet function)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: TEG platelet mapping assay provides what specific clinical value beyond standard TEG?
answer: It measures drug-induced platelet inhibition (from aspirin or ADP-pathway inhibitors like clopidogrel) with reasonable correlation to optical aggregometry, guiding decisions about platelet transfusion in patients on antiplatelet therapy.
rationale: Standard TEG reflects overall clot formation but does not quantify drug-specific platelet inhibition; the platelet mapping assay uses arachidonic acid and ADP to assess pathway-specific inhibition.
confusable_with: Standard TEG (does not measure antiplatelet drug effects)

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: During massive transfusion, heparin use is controversial. What is the current recommendation regarding heparin in massive transfusion?
answer: The use of anticoagulants such as heparin in massive transfusion remains controversial; current recommendations limit its use.
rationale: Massive trauma/hemorrhage patients often have consumptive coagulopathy; adding systemic heparin risks exacerbating bleeding; however, heparin may be needed in specific settings (e.g., to prevent circuit clotting in massive transfusion systems).

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: ABO-compatible platelet transfusions are described as desirable but not necessary. Why?
answer: Platelets have ABO antigens but transfusion of minor ABO-incompatible platelets is generally safe and effective; compatibility is preferred to reduce minor hemolysis from plasma, but it is not required for efficacy.
rationale: Red cell ABO compatibility is essential to prevent hemolytic transfusion reactions; platelet ABO compatibility improves but does not mandate platelet survival; in urgent situations incompatible platelets are acceptable.

domain: Internal medicine: hematology & oncology (anemias, anticoagulation & reversal, VTE prophylaxis & treatment, thrombocytopenia & DIC, transfusion medicine, oncologic emergencies, neutropenic fever)
stem: Hypothermia during cardiac surgery confers myocardial protection through what metabolic mechanism, and how does this relate to postoperative platelet transfusion needs?
answer: Hypothermia decreases metabolic rate 8% per 1°C, reducing myocardial oxygen demand; however, hypothermia also impairs platelet function and coagulation cascade kinetics, increasing post-CPB bleeding and platelet transfusion requirements.
rationale: Platelet adhesion, aggregation, and fibrin polymerization are temperature-dependent enzymatic processes; even mild hypothermia (34-35°C) significantly impairs hemostasis, explaining why post-CPB platelet transfusion is commonly required.
